hero.lead: Penetration testing with a focus on Linux infrastructure: servers, containers and Kubernetes – and the web applications running on them. AI-assisted reconnaissance, manual depth and a report your team can act on right away.

items.title: Linux servers & infrastructure
items.body: Exposed services, SSH, sudo and file permissions, systemd units, firewall rules and privilege escalation – from attacker shell to root.

items.title: Containers & Kubernetes
items.body: Container escapes, RBAC, network policies, secrets and images: how far does an attacker get from a compromised pod?

items.title: Web application & API pentest
items.body: Manual testing following OWASP WSTG: authentication, authorization, input validation, injection and business logic.

items.title: External attack surface
items.body: What does an attacker see from the outside? Subdomains, exposed services and forgotten systems – mapped with AI, assessed by hand.

items.title: Pipeline & supply chain
items.body: Build runners, secrets, permissions, container images and dependencies: who can push what into production?

items.title: AI applications & pipelines
items.body: LLM features following the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, agents with tool access, and the data and model pipeline behind them.

approach.lead: AI agents map your attack surface and run broad, automated tests. I verify findings by hand and follow exploitable chains in a controlled way within the agreed scope. You receive a report with reproducible evidence and concrete fixes.

steps.title: Scoping
steps.body: Goals, scope, test type (black, grey or white box) and time window agreed in writing.

steps.title: Testing
steps.body: AI-assisted reconnaissance, then manual testing. Critical findings are reported immediately, not just in the report.

steps.title: Report
steps.body: Management summary plus technical findings with reproduction steps, PoC and a concrete fix.

steps.title: Retest
steps.body: After your fixes I test again and confirm the remediation in writing.

toolbox.title: Knowing Linux from the inside to attack it from the outside
toolbox.lead: I have worked with Linux every day since 2006 – from embedded systems in medical and camera technology to build and development servers and production Kubernetes clusters. I know the systems I attack from the inside: permissions, services, configuration and the usual shortcuts in operations. For reconnaissance and reporting I use my own agent workflows; my lab is fully reproducible, and I train regularly on HackTheBox.

knowledge.title: More than prompt injection
knowledge.lead: AI applications inherit the weaknesses of classic software and add their own. Here I explain the most important risks for LLM applications and AI infrastructure – briefly, clearly and with a link to the in-depth article.
knowledge.note: Based on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 and hands-on work with agent workflows.

privacy.meta_description: Which data this website processes during a visit, and why.
privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lead: What this website records about your visit, and why. In short: no cookies, and the statistics data is not passed on to third parties.

sections.heading: Visitor statistics with GoatCounter
paragraphs: This website counts page views with GoatCounter. GoatCounter is self-hosted at stats.charemma.de on my own server.

No cookies are set and nothing is stored on your device. GoatCounter stores no IP addresses. It records the page visited, the referring page, browser and operating system, screen size and the country derived from the IP address.
The statistics data is not passed on to third parties.
The legal basis is my legitimate interest in knowing how the website is used (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR).

sections.heading: Server logs
paragraphs: A reverse proxy runs in front of the website. It logs each request with your IP address, the time, the requested domain and address, the status code, the referring page and the browser (user agent).
I use it to keep the site running, find errors, spot scans and attacks, and get a rough picture of where visits come from.

Only I evaluate the log, in a non-public view on my own server. It derives country and network (provider) from the IP address, using a database kept on the same server. The log is not passed on to third parties.

The log is not archived. It is kept only in the proxy's container log and in a temporary working directory. Both are cut once they reach a fixed size and are lost whenever the proxy restarts. There is no fixed retention period beyond that.
The legal basis is my legitimate interest in running the website securely and in knowing roughly where visits come from (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR).

sections.heading: Hosting
paragraphs: The website and the statistics run on servers of Hetzner Online GmbH in Germany (EU). Hetzner processes the data as processor.

sections.heading: Cloudflare
paragraphs: Requests to this website pass through the proxy of Cloudflare, Inc. Cloudflare processes your IP address to deliver the page and fend off attacks, and acts as processor. Cloudflare passes the IP address on to my server, where it ends up in the server log.
Cloudflare, Inc. is based in the USA, so data may be transferred to a third country. This transfer is based on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.

sections.heading: Your rights
paragraphs: You have the right of access, rectification, erasure and restriction of processing, and the right to object to processing. To exercise them, write to the e-mail address above.
You may also lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority.
